questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with fever, headache, and neck stiffness that began 8 hours ago. A lumbar puncture yields cloudy cerebrospinal fluid, and the Gram stain shows gram-negative, kidney bean-shaped organisms arranged in pairs within neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: N. meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus classically described as kidney bean- or coffee bean-shaped and is frequently seen inside neutrophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neisseria meningitidis stains gram negative and grows in pairs whose flattened adjacent sides give the kidney bean appearance. Because the organism attaches to and enters host cells, it is commonly recovered from within polymorphonuclear leukocytes on cerebrospinal fluid smears. Along with S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae it is one of the three major bacterial causes of meningitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli is a gram-negative bacillus and does not form diplococci.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. influenzae is a gram-negative coccobacillus, intermediate between a coccus and a bacillus, not a paired kidney bean form.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L. monocytogenes is a gram-positive rod and would not appear as a gram-negative diplococcus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus, so it would stain purple rather than pink on the smear.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: A gram-negative, oxidase-positive diplococcus is isolated from the cerebrospinal fluid of a college student with meningitis. The laboratory performs carbohydrate utilization testing to confirm the identification. Which of the following results is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucose and lactose fermented; maltose not fermented

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose and maltose fermented; lactose not fermented

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose fermented only; maltose not fermented

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactose and sucrose fermented; maltose not fermented

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sucrose and fructose fermented; glucose not fermented

explanation.summary: N. meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose but not lactose, sucrose, or fructose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbohydrate utilization is a standard confirmatory step for Neisseria species. N. meningitidis metabolizes both glucose and maltose, while lactose, sucrose, and fructose are not fermented. Combined with an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus on smear, this pattern identifies the organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactose is not fermented by this organism, and maltose is.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose fermentation alone is incomplete, because maltose is also fermented.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactose and sucrose are both negative, and maltose is positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neither sucrose nor fructose is fermented, and glucose is.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: A cerebrospinal fluid isolate is being characterized to confirm a diagnosis of meningococcal meningitis. Which of the following sets of laboratory characteristics is expected for this organism?

explanation.summary: N. meningitidis is oxidase positive, nonmotile, nonhemolytic, and facultatively anaerobic, with growth optimized in 5% carbon dioxide.
explanation.whyCorrect: A positive oxidase reaction is a defining screening test for Neisseria species. The organism does not move on its own and produces no hemolysis on blood-containing media. It is facultatively anaerobic and grows best in an atmosphere enriched to 5% carbon dioxide.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The organism is oxidase positive, nonmotile, and produces no hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The oxidase test is positive and the organism is nonmotile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The oxidase test is positive, and no alpha-hemolysis is produced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although oxidase positive, the organism is nonmotile and nonhemolytic.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: During an outbreak investigation, nasopharyngeal swabs are collected from asymptomatic students to look for meningococcal carriage. Because the specimens come from a site heavily colonized with normal flora, which of the following media should be used to recover the organism?

explanation.summary: Thayer-Martin agar is the selective medium used when a Neisseria specimen comes from a nonsterile site.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thayer-Martin agar is built on a chocolate agar base, with antibiotics, antifungals, and added nutrients that suppress competing flora while supporting Neisseria. That selectivity is what makes it the right choice for a nonsterile specimen such as a nasopharyngeal swab. Specimens from sterile sites, such as cerebrospinal fluid, can simply be plated on chocolate agar.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood agar is differential rather than selective and does not adequately support this fastidious organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MacConkey agar is used for gram-negative enteric organisms and to assess lactose fermentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mannitol salt agar is a high-salt medium used to select for staphylococci, not Neisseria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An unsupplemented nutrient broth is neither enriched nor selective and would be overgrown by normal flora.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: A microbiology student asks why fastidious organisms such as Neisseria species grow well on chocolate agar. Which of the following best explains this property of the medium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 7.5% sodium chloride concentration enriches for cocci

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibiotics and antifungals suppress competing organisms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bile salts and crystal violet select for gram-negative rods

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactose and a pH indicator reveal fermenting colonies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cells are heat-lysed, releasing added nutrients

explanation.summary: Chocolate agar is red blood cell agar that has been heated to lyse the cells and release intracellular nutrients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fastidious bacteria require an enriched medium. Heating blood agar ruptures the erythrocytes, spilling their contents into the medium and raising nutrient availability, which also gives the agar its brown chocolate color. Both N. meningitidis and H. influenzae grow on it for this reason.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high salt concentration describes mannitol salt agar, which selects for staphylococci.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Added antimicrobials describe the selective Thayer-Martin formulation, not chocolate agar itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bile salts and crystal violet describe MacConkey agar, a selective medium for enteric gram-negative rods.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactose with a pH indicator is a differential feature of media such as MacConkey agar.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: The endotoxin of N. meningitidis is designated lipooligosaccharide rather than lipopolysaccharide. Compared with the lipopolysaccharide of most other gram-negative bacteria, this molecule differs in which of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a secreted exotoxin rather than a wall component

choices.label: B
choices.text: It lacks lipid A and therefore triggers no cytokine release

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lacks the core polysaccharide, leaving only lipid A

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lacks the O antigen, making a shorter molecule

choices.label: E
choices.text: It sits in the inner rather than the outer membrane

explanation.summary: Meningococcal endotoxin is a lipooligosaccharide because it lacks the O antigen found in typical gram-negative lipopolysaccharide.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typical lipopolysaccharide has three parts: lipid A (the toxic component), a core polysaccharide, and an O antigen. N. meningitidis omits the O antigen, producing the shorter lipooligosaccharide. It still functions as an endotoxin, triggering immunologic responses and a potential cytokine storm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It is a structural membrane endotoxin, not a secreted exotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipid A is retained and is precisely what makes the molecule toxic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The core polysaccharide remains; it is the O antigen that is missing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The molecule remains an outer membrane component, as in other gram-negative organisms.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: The polysaccharide capsule of N. meningitidis carries the antigens used to divide the species into serogroups. Which of the following groups includes the most common pathogenic serogroups?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serogroups a, b, c, d, e, and f

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serogroups A, B, C, X, Y, and W-135

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serogroups D, E, F, G, H, and I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serogroups I, II, III, IV, V, and VI

explanation.summary: Capsular antigens define meningococcal serogroups A, B, C, X, Y, and W-135 as the most common pathogenic groups.
explanation.whyCorrect: Specific antigens within the polysaccharide capsule determine the serogroup. A, B, C, X, Y, and W-135 account for the pathogenic strains, with B, C, Y, and W-135 the most common causes of disease and serogroup A notable for causing epidemics. Vaccines are directed at these capsular antigens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Numeric designations are not used for meningococcal capsular serogroups.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lowercase serotypes a through f describe encapsulated H. influenzae, not N. meningitidis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These letters are not the recognized pathogenic meningococcal serogroups.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Roman numeral designations are not used for meningococcal capsular serogroups.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl received the quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) at her last visit. Her mother asks whether any pathogenic meningococcal serogroup remains uncovered by that vaccine. Which of the following serogroups requires a separate vaccine?

explanation.summary: MenACWY does not protect against serogroup B, which requires a separate recombinant protein vaccine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The quadrivalent conjugate vaccine covers serogroups A, C, W-135, and Y but not B. A separate recombinant protein vaccine against serogroup B is available in the United States for children 10 years of age and older. A pentavalent product, MenABCWY, covers all five serogroups in one vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Serogroup A is one of the four serogroups included in MenACWY.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serogroup C is included in the quadrivalent conjugate vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serogroup W-135 is the W component of MenACWY.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serogroup Y is the Y component of MenACWY.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: A healthy child is seen for a routine health maintenance visit, and the parents ask when the meningococcal conjugate vaccine series should begin. Routine vaccination is recommended starting at which of the following ages, with a booster at 16 years?

explanation.summary: Routine meningococcal conjugate vaccination is given at 11 to 12 years of age with a booster at age 16.
explanation.whyCorrect: Conjugated vaccines developed against meningococcal capsular antigens are recommended for adolescents at 11 to 12 years, followed by a booster at 16 years. This timing precedes the second disease peak at 18 to 25 years, when close quarters such as dormitories and military camps increase risk. By contrast, H. influenzae type b vaccination begins at 2 months of age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two months is when the Hib series begins, not meningococcal vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ages 4 to 6 years fall before the recommended adolescent start.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Twelve months is earlier than the recommended start of routine meningococcal vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting until 18 to 21 years would leave adolescents unprotected through the rising-risk years.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: N. meningitidis first establishes itself by binding nonciliated nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, endothelium, and erythrocytes. Which of the following pairs of surface structures mediates this attachment?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Opacity proteins and type IV pili

explanation.summary: Opacity proteins and type IV pili are the attachment and invasion factors of N. meningitidis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opacity proteins allow the organism to adhere to human cells, and type IV pili bind nonciliated nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, endothelium, and erythrocytes. The pili also aggregate bacteria into units that move across the surface by twitching motility. These adhesins are the first step toward colonization and later invasion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cord factor is a mycobacterial lipid and is not an adhesin of this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: N. meningitidis is nonmotile and has no flagella; M protein is a streptococcal factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipoteichoic acid is a gram-positive wall component and mycolic acid is found in mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein A and coagulase are staphylococcal virulence factors.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: After N. meningitidis pili aggregate the bacteria into units that migrate across the nasopharyngeal surface by twitching motility, the organism binds host cell microvilli. Which of the following best describes what happens next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enters in vesicles and spreads to adjacent cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It forms spores that persist within the mucosal layer

choices.label: C
choices.text: It multiplies only inside erythrocytes after lysing them

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes an exotoxin that lyses cells from the outside

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stays extracellular and is rapidly cleared by neutrophils

explanation.summary: N. meningitidis is a facultative intracellular organism that enters cells in membrane-bound vesicles and destroys them as it spreads.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacterial units bind microvilli and enter the cell inside membrane-bound vesicles. Once intracellular, the organism migrates through the cytoplasm into adjacent cells, destroying them in the process. This facultative intracellular lifestyle also lets it reside within polymorphonuclear leukocytes, which is why it is seen inside neutrophils on smears.

whyWrongByChoice.B: N. meningitidis does not form spores.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It binds erythrocytes but does not replicate exclusively within them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Its principal toxin is the membrane-bound lipooligosaccharide endotoxin, not a secreted cytolytic exotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The organism survives inside polymorphonuclear leukocytes rather than being simply cleared by them.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: Both N. meningitidis and H. influenzae colonize the nasopharynx in part by degrading the antibody that guards mucosal surfaces. Which of the following virulence factors is responsible?

explanation.summary: IgA protease cleaves secretory IgA and allows both organisms to colonize the nasopharynx.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgA is the dominant immunoglobulin at mucosal surfaces. Both N. meningitidis and H. influenzae produce an IgA protease that cleaves it, which is why each can establish nasopharyngeal colonization. S. pneumoniae, the third major cause of acute meningitis, also produces this enzyme.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipooligosaccharide acts as an endotoxin that drives inflammation rather than cleaving IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opacity proteins mediate attachment to human cells, not antibody destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The capsule blocks phagocytosis and complement but does not degrade antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type IV pili bind epithelium, endothelium, and erythrocytes but have no protease activity.

questions.topicName: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae

questions.stem: A hospital microbiology laboratory receives several gram-negative bacillary isolates from urine, blood, and stool cultures. All of them grow well on MacConkey agar, but the technologist notes that they differ from one another in motility, urease activity, and the speed with which they turn the medium pink. Which property is shared by all members of the Enterobacteriaceae family?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They all ferment glucose to acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: They all hydrolyze urea to ammonia

choices.label: D
choices.text: They all produce hydrogen sulfide on TSI agar

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are all motile by means of flagella

explanation.summary: Every member of the Enterobacteriaceae ferments glucose; lactose fermentation, motility, urease, and H2S are what separate the genera.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucose fermentation is the common denominator of the family, which is why the differential media used for these organisms focus on lactose rather than glucose. MacConkey agar separates the family into lactose fermenters and non-fermenters, and additional tests such as motility, urease, and H2S production narrow the identification to a genus. This is the basis of the gram-negative lab algorithm used to work up an enteric isolate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Proteus, Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia do not turn MacConkey pink, and Citrobacter ferments lactose only slowly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E. coli and Serratia are urease negative, which helps separate them from Proteus and Klebsiella.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only Salmonella, Proteus, and Citrobacter produce H2S; E. coli and K. pneumoniae do not.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Klebsiella and Shigella are nonmotile and grow only along the stab line in a motility tube.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A gram-negative bacillus isolated from a hospitalized patient's urine produces colorless colonies on MacConkey agar at 24 hours, but by 72 hours the colonies and surrounding medium have taken on a faint pink color. The isolate is motile, urease positive, blackens the butt of a TSI tube, and produces no pigment. Which organism is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Citrobacter is a slow lactose fermenter that is motile, urease positive, and produces H2S.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fast lactose fermenters change the color of MacConkey agar within 24 to 48 hours, while slow fermenters take beyond 48 hours and produce a less intense pink. Citrobacter is one of the slow fermenters, and it is additionally motile, urease positive, and an H2S producer. That combination distinguishes it from the other common enteric genera.

whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is a fast lactose fermenter that is urease negative and does not produce H2S.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella is a fast lactose fermenter, is nonmotile, and forms mucoid colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus does not ferment lactose at all, so its colonies remain colorless indefinitely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia is urease negative and produces the red pigment prodigiosin.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A stool specimen is plated onto eosin methylene blue (EMB) agar. After overnight incubation, the technologist reports colonies with a striking green metallic sheen. Which organism is most likely present?

explanation.summary: A green metallic sheen on EMB agar is the classic appearance of E. coli.
explanation.whyCorrect: EMB agar contains eosin and methylene blue, which inhibit gram-positive organisms and stain lactose-fermenting bacteria black. E. coli is the exception: it interacts with the dyes to form colonies with a characteristic green metallic sheen. This finding is used together with lactose fermentation and beta-hemolysis to identify E. coli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrobacter ferments lactose slowly and does not develop a metallic sheen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterobacter ferments lactose and stains black on EMB like the other fermenters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klebsiella ferments lactose and therefore appears black on EMB, not metallic green.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella does not ferment lactose, so it forms colorless colonies on this medium.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A urine culture from a patient with a long-term indwelling catheter grows a gram-negative rod that spreads across the plate in concentric waves rather than as discrete colonies. The isolate produces colorless colonies on MacConkey agar, is strongly urease positive, and blackens the butt of a TSI tube. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Swarming motility with urease and H2S production in a non-lactose fermenter identifies Proteus mirabilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Proteus mirabilis is motile in a unique swarming pattern that spreads over the agar surface. It does not ferment lactose, it is urease positive, and it is one of the enteric organisms that produces H2S on TSI agar. This triad separates it from the other genera in the family.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli ferments lactose, is urease negative, and does not produce H2S.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Klebsiella is nonmotile with mucoid colonies and does not produce H2S.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serratia is urease negative and produces red pigment rather than swarming growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella is nonmotile and does not produce H2S on TSI agar.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: Sputum from a patient with pneumonia grows a gram-negative rod that forms large, glistening, mucoid colonies. The organism turns MacConkey agar deep pink within 24 hours, shows no migration away from the stab in a motility tube, and is urease positive. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Mucoid colonies from a nonmotile, urease-positive fast lactose fermenter point to Klebsiella pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Klebsiella pneumoniae ferments lactose rapidly, so MacConkey agar turns pink within 24 to 48 hours. It is one of only two enteric organisms in this group that are nonmotile, and it is urease positive. Its mucoid colonies reflect its abundant capsule and are a recognized clue on the plate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterobacter is motile and only weakly urease positive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is motile, urease negative, and shows a green sheen on EMB rather than mucoid growth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus does not ferment lactose and displays swarming motility.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salmonella does not ferment lactose and is motile.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: An intensive care unit isolate from a respiratory specimen is a motile gram-negative rod whose colonies develop a deep red pigment after incubation at room temperature. The organism is urease negative. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Red prodigiosin pigment from a motile, urease-negative enteric rod identifies Serratia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serratia species produce the red pigment prodigiosin, which is their single most recognizable laboratory feature. They are motile and urease negative, which separates them from Proteus, Klebsiella, and Citrobacter. Serratia is one of the enteric opportunists that becomes prominent in hospitalized patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrobacter is urease positive and produces no pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli produces no pigment and shows a green metallic sheen on EMB agar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella is nonmotile and urease positive, and its colonies are mucoid rather than red.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus is urease positive, produces H2S, and swarms across the plate.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A laboratory performs motility testing by stabbing several enteric isolates into tubes of solid agar. Two of the isolates grow only along the narrow inoculation tract, while the rest cloud the surrounding agar. Which pair of organisms is expected to remain confined to the stab line?

explanation.summary: Among the enteric organisms, Klebsiella and Shigella are the nonmotile ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Motility is tested by piercing solid agar in a test tube; motile organisms migrate beyond the inoculated area and cloud the medium, while nonmotile organisms stay within the tract. E. coli, Salmonella, Serratia, Proteus, and some Citrobacter are motile. Klebsiella and Shigella lack this ability and therefore produce growth only along the stab.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both E. coli and Salmonella are motile and will cloud the agar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proteus is not only motile but swarms, and Serratia is motile as well.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salmonella is motile, and at least some Citrobacter isolates are motile.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia and E. coli are both motile organisms.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A stool isolate from a patient with fever and diarrhea is inoculated onto triple sugar iron (TSI) agar. After incubation, the butt of the tube has turned black. Which organism is most consistent with this result?

explanation.summary: Blackening of TSI agar indicates H2S production, which among these organisms only Salmonella performs.
explanation.whyCorrect: TSI agar contains sodium thiosulfate and ferrous sulfate, and H2S produced by the organism reacts with the iron salt to deposit black ferrous sulfide. Salmonella, Proteus, and Citrobacter are the H2S producers in this family. The gram-negative lab algorithm uses this step to separate Salmonella and Proteus from Shigella and Yersinia among the non-lactose fermenters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli does not produce H2S, so the butt of the tube would not blacken.
whyWrongByChoice.B: K. pneumoniae is explicitly H2S negative and also ferments lactose rapidly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shigella falls on the H2S-negative branch of the enteric algorithm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia is also an H2S-negative non-lactose fermenter.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A student examines a TSI tube in which the deep portion of the medium has become jet black after overnight incubation of an enteric isolate. Which chemical reaction accounts for this appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gas produced by fermentation darkens the agar as it cracks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrogen sulfide reacts with ferrous sulfate to form ferrous sulfide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phenol red is reduced to a dark pigment under acidic conditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prodigiosin made by the organism diffuses through the agar

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urease hydrolyzes urea and alkalinizes the deep part of the tube

explanation.summary: The black color of TSI agar is insoluble ferrous sulfide precipitated from bacterial H2S.
explanation.whyCorrect: TSI agar contains sodium thiosulfate as a sulfur source and ferrous sulfate as an indicator. Organisms that reduce thiosulfate generate H2S, which reacts with the ferrous salt to form ferrous sulfide, an insoluble black precipitate. Sugar fermentation, gas production, and H2S production are read together to separate members of the family.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gas production is read as cracks or bubbles in the agar, not as a color change.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenol red is the pH indicator in TSI and turns yellow with acid, never black.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prodigiosin is the red pigment of Serratia and has nothing to do with the TSI reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urease activity is tested separately and does not generate a black precipitate.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: An enteric isolate is inoculated onto TSI agar. Before inoculation the medium is red; after incubation both the slant and the butt of the tube are bright yellow. What does this color change indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism fermented one or more sugars to acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism hydrolyzed urea and raised the pH

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism is nonmotile and stayed along the stab

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism produced gas that cracked the agar

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism produced hydrogen sulfide from thiosulfate

explanation.summary: Yellow TSI agar means a sugar was fermented and the resulting acid turned phenol red yellow.
explanation.whyCorrect: TSI contains lactose, sucrose, and glucose along with phenol red, a pH-sensitive dye that gives the medium its red color. When any of these sugars is fermented, the environment becomes acidic and phenol red turns yellow. Reading the slant and the butt separately shows which sugars were used.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alkalinization would move phenol red away from yellow, not toward it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Motility is assessed in a separate soft agar tube, not by TSI color.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gas production is read as cracks or bubbles within the agar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H2S production is signaled by a black precipitate, not by a yellow color.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A blood agar plate inoculated with an enteric gram-negative rod shows a zone of complete clearing of the red blood cells around the colonies. Among the common members of Enterobacteriaceae, which organism is expected to produce this pattern?

explanation.summary: E. coli is the only beta-hemolytic organism among the Enterobacteriaceae discussed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complete clearing of red cells around a colony is beta-hemolysis. Of the enteric organisms covered, only E. coli is beta-hemolytic on blood agar. Because the rest of the family is not hemolytic, hemolysis patterns are otherwise not used to distinguish between members of Enterobacteriaceae.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Klebsiella is not beta-hemolytic; it is recognized by mucoid, lactose-fermenting colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proteus is not beta-hemolytic; its clue on agar is swarming growth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serratia is not beta-hemolytic; its clue is red prodigiosin pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella is not beta-hemolytic and forms colorless colonies on MacConkey agar.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man develops fever, hypotension, and tachypnea 12 hours after a gram-negative rod is recovered from his blood. Cytokine-driven systemic inflammation is thought to be responsible for his presentation. Which bacterial component is the principal trigger of this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fimbriae used for attachment to host cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flagellar H antigen on the cell surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peptidoglycan of the inner cell wall layer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polysaccharide K1 capsule of the organism

explanation.summary: LPS in the gram-negative outer membrane is the endotoxin that drives inflammation and sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A major virulence factor of gram-negative bacteria, including E. coli, is the LPS found in the outer membrane of the cell wall. LPS is notorious for provoking inflammatory responses that can progress to sepsis. Its three parts are the O-specific polysaccharide, the core polysaccharide, and lipid A.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fimbriae mediate attachment to host surfaces rather than systemic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The H antigen is a flagellar protein used for strain typing, not an endotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peptidoglycan is a structural component and is not the endotoxin described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The K1 capsule promotes immune evasion in neonatal meningitis, not endotoxic shock.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever to 103.6°F (39.8°C), productive cough, worsening shortness of breath, and pleuritic chest pain. She is a college student who binge drinks heavily and consumed more than seven drinks at a party the previous weekend. Her sputum is thick, sticky, and reddish. A chest radiograph shows dense consolidation of the right upper lobe. Sputum Gram stain shows gram-negative bacilli, and culture grows mucoid, lactose-fermenting, indole-negative colonies. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Thick, sticky "red currant jelly" sputum in a patient with alcohol use disorder, together with mucoid lactose-fermenting indole-negative colonies, identifies Klebsiella pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: K. pneumoniae is part of the normal flora of the gastrointestinal tract and causes pneumonia most often in hospitalized patients and in people with alcohol use disorder, because aspiration of oral and gastrointestinal contents is common after heavy drinking. Its large mucoid polysaccharide capsule makes the sputum thick, sticky, and reddish, the classic "red currant jelly sputum." In the laboratory it is a gram-negative rod that ferments lactose rapidly but does not produce indole, and its colonies are visibly mucoid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli also ferments lactose rapidly, but it is indole positive and its colonies are not mucoid, and it does not produce currant jelly sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: P. mirabilis does not ferment lactose and causes urinary tract infections far more often than pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serratia ferments lactose only slowly and is a minor cause of respiratory infection, usually in immunocompromised hosts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus, which does not fit the gram-negative bacilli seen on this patient's sputum Gram stain.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old hospitalized man with alcohol use disorder has lobar pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. His expectorated sputum is thick, sticky, and reddish, which the attending physician describes to the team as "red currant jelly" sputum. Which of the following bacterial structures is most directly responsible for this sputum appearance?

explanation.summary: The currant jelly appearance of Klebsiella sputum comes from the organism's large mucoid polysaccharide capsule.
explanation.whyCorrect: K. pneumoniae produces an unusually large mucoid polysaccharide capsule. Shed into the airway secretions, this capsular material gives the sputum a thick, sticky, slimy consistency, which combined with blood gives the reddish currant jelly appearance. The same capsule makes colonies on agar look slimy, as though someone blew their nose on the plate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-lactamase is a secreted antibiotic-inactivating enzyme and plays no part in the appearance of sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipopolysaccharide is the endotoxin that drives fever and the septic response; it does not change sputum consistency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: K. pneumoniae is nonmotile, so flagella are not a feature of this organism at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fimbriae mediate adherence to host epithelium and have no effect on the viscosity of secretions.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man in the intensive care unit has been mechanically ventilated for 8 days when he develops fever, purulent secretions, and a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Endotracheal aspirate grows a gram-negative bacillus that is also a normal inhabitant of his gastrointestinal tract. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia, particularly in ventilated patients, and it comes from the patient's own gut flora.
explanation.whyCorrect: Members of the Enterobacteriaceae, especially E. coli and K. pneumoniae, are among the most common causes of hospital-acquired infection, and K. pneumoniae is a leading cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia. Because it colonizes the gastrointestinal tract normally, a hospitalized patient can be infected by his own flora as well as by contaminated equipment or staff hands. Sepsis may follow as a complication of the pneumonia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspergillus is a mold, not a gram-negative bacillus, and is not a gastrointestinal commensal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: B. pertussis is a coccobacillus causing whooping cough in the community, not ventilator-associated pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Legionella is a ventilator-associated pathogen but is acquired from contaminated water systems, not from the patient's gut flora.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall and cannot be seen as a gram-negative bacillus on Gram stain.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: Two gram-negative bacilli isolated from separate hospitalized patients both ferment lactose rapidly on MacConkey agar. Tryptophan-containing broth is inoculated with each isolate and a color-change reagent is added: isolate 1 develops a red layer at the surface, while isolate 2 remains yellow. Isolate 1 is most likely which of the following?

explanation.summary: The indole test separates the two rapid lactose fermenters: E. coli makes indole from tryptophan and K. pneumoniae does not.
explanation.whyCorrect: The indole test detects whether an organism can produce indole from tryptophan; a color-change reagent turns red when indole is present. E. coli is indole positive, so isolate 1 is E. coli. This is one of the standard ways to tell E. coli from K. pneumoniae, since both are gram-negative rods that ferment lactose quickly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterobacter ferments lactose rapidly but is indole negative, which is exactly what distinguishes it from E. coli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: K. pneumoniae does not produce indole from tryptophan, so it would give the yellow result seen with isolate 2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P. mirabilis is indole negative and also does not ferment lactose, so it fails both parts of the description.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia ferments lactose only slowly, so it does not match the rapid fermentation described in the stem.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A laboratory technologist stabs semi-solid motility agar with five different Enterobacteriaceae isolates. Four of them produce diffuse, hazy growth spreading well away from the stab line; one grows only along the line of inoculation. The isolate that grew only along the stab line is most likely which of the following?

explanation.summary: Among the common Enterobacteriaceae, Klebsiella is the nonmotile one; growth confined to the stab line means no motility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Strains of Klebsiella are usually nonmotile, so they cannot spread away from the point of inoculation in semi-solid agar and growth stays along the stab line. This is a useful additional way to separate K. pneumoniae from E. coli, which is motile, and it is one of the features listed for Klebsiella alongside its mucoid capsule and indole-negative reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterobacter species are motile and would also produce diffuse growth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is motile and would produce the diffuse growth away from the stab line.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P. mirabilis is the most motile organism in this group and swarms vigorously across agar surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia species are motile and would spread through semi-solid agar.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A MacConkey agar plate inoculated with a tracheal aspirate from a hospitalized patient grows pink colonies that are strikingly slimy and string out when touched with an inoculating loop. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: Pink (lactose-fermenting) colonies that are distinctly mucoid and slimy on MacConkey agar are characteristic of Klebsiella pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both E. coli and K. pneumoniae have a capsule, but the Klebsiella capsule is mucoid, so its colonies look very slimy in culture. Combined with pink color from lactose fermentation, this mucoid colony appearance is a practical way to pick K. pneumoniae out from other lactose fermenters at the bench.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli ferments lactose and turns pink on MacConkey agar, but its colonies are not mucoid or stringy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: P. mirabilis does not ferment lactose, so its colonies remain colorless on MacConkey agar.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pseudomonas does not ferment lactose and would not produce pink colonies on this medium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella does not ferment lactose and forms colorless, non-mucoid colonies.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A blood isolate of Klebsiella pneumoniae from a hospitalized patient is resistant to ampicillin and to ceftriaxone, and the laboratory reports the strain as an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producer. Which of the following best describes the activity of the responsible enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acetylates chloramphenicol so the drug can no longer bind ribosomes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring of penicillins and cephalosporins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It methylates the 30S ribosomal subunit so aminoglycosides cannot bind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It pumps fluoroquinolone molecules out of the bacterial cytoplasm.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It substitutes an altered penicillin-binding protein into the cell wall.

explanation.summary: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases are enzymes that break down commonly used beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillins and cephalosporins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rates of resistance to penicillin and cephalosporin among the Enterobacteriaceae have risen substantially over the last decade, and strains carrying these enzymes are collectively called ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae. The enzymes destroy the beta-lactam ring, rendering penicillins and cephalosporins ineffective, so providers must fall back on intravenous carbapenems for infections that used to be treated with oral agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylation of chloramphenicol is a separate enzymatic resistance mechanism unrelated to beta-lactam drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ribosomal methylation is an aminoglycoside resistance mechanism and would not confer resistance to penicillins or cephalosporins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Efflux pumps expel drugs such as fluoroquinolones; they are not what the term beta-lactamase describes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An altered penicillin-binding protein is the basis of methicillin resistance in staphylococci, not of ESBL production.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with no chronic medical problems, no recent hospitalization, and no indwelling devices is found to have a urinary tract infection caused by an ESBL-producing Escherichia coli. A medical student is surprised that a healthy outpatient could acquire such an organism. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About one in four patients with an ESBL infection has no known underlying health condition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: ESBL infections arise only after a patient completes a prolonged course of carbapenems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: ESBL production is restricted to Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter rather than Enterobacteriaceae.

choices.label: D
choices.text: ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae have steadily declined in the United States since 2012.

choices.label: E
choices.text: ESBL-producing organisms are essentially confined to ICU patients with indwelling devices.

explanation.summary: ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae are a concern in the community as well as in health care, and roughly a quarter of infected patients have no known underlying illness.
explanation.whyCorrect: What is particularly problematic about ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae is that they infect otherwise healthy patients at an alarming rate: about one out of four patients with an ESBL infection has no known underlying health condition. These organisms spread rapidly and can cause or complicate infections in healthy people as well as in health care settings, which is why they carry a serious threat rating.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbapenem exposure selects for carbapenem resistance; ESBL infections occur without any such prior therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ESBL is by definition a property of Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli and K. pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cases of ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae have increased since 2012, not declined.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ESBL-producing organisms are a documented concern in the community, not just among device-associated ICU patients.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 71-year-old hospitalized man has bacteremia caused by an ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. Susceptibility testing shows resistance to ceftriaxone, cefepime, ampicillin, and piperacillin. Which of the following intravenous agents is the most appropriate treatment?

explanation.summary: ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae can still be treated with carbapenems, which is why providers must often switch from oral agents to intravenous carbapenem therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibiotic options for ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae are limited because the enzyme destroys penicillins and cephalosporins. Health care providers therefore often have to use intravenous carbapenem antibiotics, such as meropenem, to treat infections that would previously have been managed with oral drugs. The downside is that heavier carbapenem use is itself driving the rise of carbapenem-resistant strains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is an oral penicillin combination and is not adequate for an ESBL bloodstream infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ampicillin-sulbactam is a penicillin combination and falls within the spectrum of drugs the enzyme destroys.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cefoxitin is a cephalosporin and therefore shares the same vulnerability to the enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ceftazidime is a cephalosporin and is inactivated by the extended-spectrum beta-lactamase.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: An infection-control team is reviewing carbapenem resistance among Enterobacteriaceae isolates at their hospital. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbapenem resistance develops only in strains that do not also produce ESBL enzymes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbapenem resistance has been essentially eliminated from United States hospitals since 2012.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbapenem resistance is confined to community-acquired rather than nosocomial isolates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Carbapenem resistance is far more common in Escherichia coli than in Klebsiella pneumoniae.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Roughly 11% of nosocomial Klebsiella pneumoniae infections are carbapenem resistant.

explanation.summary: Although both E. coli and K. pneumoniae can be carbapenem resistant, resistance is much more common in K. pneumoniae, about 11% of nosocomial isolates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased use of carbapenems to treat ESBL infections has driven a rise in carbapenem resistance. Both E. coli and K. pneumoniae can be carbapenem resistant, but resistance is much more common in K. pneumoniae, with roughly 11% of all nosocomial K. pneumoniae infections carbapenem resistant. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae carry an urgent threat rating.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ESBL production and carbapenem resistance frequently coexist; in fact carbapenem use to treat ESBL strains selects for the latter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbapenem resistance remains a major concern in United States health care facilities and has not been eliminated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae are principally a problem of health care facilities, not the community.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The relationship is the reverse: carbapenem resistance is much more common in K. pneumoniae than in E. coli.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 74-year-old hospitalized woman with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and a central venous catheter develops bacteremia with a carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) isolate. Her family asks about her prognosis. Mortality from CRE infection in hospitalized patients with comorbidities has been reported to be as high as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Mortality from carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae infection has been reported as high as 50% in hospitalized patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae are resistant to nearly all available antibiotics, leaving only more toxic or less effective treatment options. Mortality can be extremely high, especially in hospitalized patients with comorbidities, and has been reported as high as 50% in hospitalized patients who contract CRE infections. This severity is why CRE is designated an urgent threat.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 1% mortality figure greatly underestimates the lethality of CRE infection in comorbid hospitalized patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 5% mortality figure is far below the reported rate for CRE infections in this population.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 15% mortality figure still substantially understates the reported CRE mortality in hospitalized patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 90% mortality figure overstates the reported rate; even in the sickest hospitalized patients it reaches about 50%.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: On one hospital ward, unrelated isolates of Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterobacter cloacae are all found to carry the same carbapenemase gene. Which of the following best explains how this resistance gene moved among these different species?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A spontaneous chromosomal point mutation arose independently within each species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each species sporulated and passed the gene along within a resistant spore coat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gene integrated into human host DNA and was later returned to the bacteria.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gene was carried on a plasmid and transferred between cells by conjugation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gene was displayed on the bacterial capsule and swapped during cell clumping.

explanation.summary: Antibiotic resistance genes in the Enterobacteriaceae are usually carried on plasmids that move between bacteria by conjugation.
explanation.whyCorrect: These antibiotic resistance genes are usually encoded on a plasmid that transfers between bacteria via conjugation, which is why the identical gene can appear in several different genera on the same ward. Other forms of horizontal transfer may also contribute to the spread. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae in particular carry mobile genetic elements that are easily shared between bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Independent identical point mutations in three separate species is vanishingly unlikely and would not produce one shared gene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterobacteriaceae are not spore formers, so spore-mediated transfer is not possible for these organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bacterial resistance genes are not routed through human genomic DNA on their way between bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsule is a protective polysaccharide layer and is not a vehicle for exchanging genes.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman has an 11-day history of facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, and fever. Examination shows maxillary sinus tenderness, and acute bacterial sinusitis is diagnosed. Which of the following groups of organisms is most likely responsible for her infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Proteus mirabilis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Listeria monocytogenes, Enterococcus faecalis, and Clostridioides difficile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Rickettsia rickettsii

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Serratia marcescens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis

explanation.summary: Acute bacterial sinusitis is usually caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and M. catarrhalis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute bacterial sinusitis is an upper respiratory tract infection, and the three organisms that classically cause it are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. This trio drives the choice of therapy, which must cover a gram-positive coccus plus two gram-negative respiratory organisms. Amoxicillin/clavulanate is therefore a very common treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These Enterobacteriaceae cause urinary and intra-abdominal infections, not the typical upper respiratory tract picture of sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Listeria, Enterococcus, and C. difficile cause meningitis, urinary tract infection, and colitis respectively, not sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These atypical and rickettsial organisms cause atypical pneumonia, genital infection, and tick-borne illness rather than bacterial sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These are hospital-associated gram-negative organisms seen in ventilated or severely ill patients, not causes of community sinusitis.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man is diagnosed with acute bacterial sinusitis and needs an oral antibiotic that will cover Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?

explanation.summary: Amoxicillin/clavulanate is the common treatment for acute bacterial sinusitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin, when combined with a β-lactamase inhibitor like clavulanate, provide good gram-positive coverage plus good gram-negative coverage. That combination spans S. pneumoniae as well as H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis, which are the organisms of acute bacterial sinusitis. It is therefore a very common outpatient choice for this infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside with limited gram-positive activity and is not an oral agent for sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbapenems are reserved for complicated infections such as hospital-acquired pneumonia and are not oral agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Linezolid covers gram-positive organisms only and provides no coverage of the gram-negative respiratory pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin that is not effective against many gram-negative bacteria such as H. influenzae.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student is admitted with fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity. Cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci, and cultures grow Neisseria meningitidis. Which of the following antibiotics has activity against this organism?

explanation.summary: Ampicillin combined with sulbactam is effective against Neisseria meningitidis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminopenicillins paired with a β-lactamase inhibitor extend their reach into gram-negative organisms. Ampicillin with sulbactam is specifically effective against Neisseria meningitidis, which causes bacterial meningitis and septicemia. The other listed agents act only on gram-positive bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Linezolid is a gram-positive agent and would not treat a gram-negative diplococcus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not effective against many gram-negative bacteria, including Neisseria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed, acts only in the gut, and has no gram-negative activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxacillin, like nafcillin, is aimed at staphylococci and lacks gram-negative coverage.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a urinary tract infection, and ampicillin is started. Aminopenicillins retain useful gram-positive activity with one important exception. Which of the following organisms is reliably covered by ampicillin?

explanation.summary: Aminopenicillins cover gram-positive organisms including Enterococcus, but not MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amoxicillin and ampicillin provide good gram-positive coverage, and Enterococcus is specifically included in that spectrum. The single gram-positive exception is MRSA, which aminopenicillins do not cover. Enterococcal urinary tract infection is therefore a classic ampicillin indication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acinetobacter is a resistant gram-negative organism outside the aminopenicillin spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing Enterobacteriaceae are explicitly not covered by aminopenicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MRSA is the named gram-positive exception to aminopenicillin coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminopenicillins, even with a β-lactamase inhibitor, do not cover Pseudomonas.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 70-year-old hospitalized woman with a catheter-associated urinary tract infection is treated with ampicillin-sulbactam but remains febrile. Urine culture grows an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminopenicillins act only on organisms growing anaerobically

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aminopenicillins are excreted unchanged and never reach the urine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aminopenicillins cover only atypical intracellular pathogens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aminopenicillins do not cover ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aminopenicillins inhibit the 30S ribosome rather than the cell wall

explanation.summary: Aminopenicillins fail against ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae and against Pseudomonas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amoxicillin and ampicillin, even with a β-lactamase inhibitor, do not cover extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing Enterobacteriaceae or Pseudomonas. ESBL organisms make β-lactamase enzymes that degrade these β-lactam antibiotics. Carbapenems are the reliable option once an ESBL producer is identified.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminopenicillins are not restricted to anaerobic growth conditions; E. coli grows aerobically and is ordinarily within their spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Drug delivery to the urine is not the problem here; enzymatic degradation of the antibiotic is.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aminopenicillins with an inhibitor cover many atypicals but are not limited to them; they are primarily cell-wall active agents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminopenicillins are β-lactams that block cell wall synthesis; 30S inhibition describes aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in the intensive care unit develops fever and hypotension three days after abdominal surgery. Broad empiric coverage of gram-positive organisms, Enterobacteriaceae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is needed while cultures are pending. Which of the following single agents is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam has one of the broadest gram-negative spectra and is used for initial empiric therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam has broad gram-positive coverage (except MRSA) together with one of the broadest gram-negative coverages, including Enterobacter, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, Proteus, ESBL producers, and Pseudomonas. That breadth is exactly why it is chosen for initial empiric therapy in a septic post-surgical patient. No other listed agent spans gram-positives and Pseudomonas at once.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ampicillin-sulbactam does not cover Pseudomonas or ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aztreonam treats only aerobic gram-negative bacteria and would leave gram-positive organisms uncovered.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is not effective against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and has limited activity against anaerobes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin with no meaningful gram-negative activity.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A patient with a complicated intra-abdominal infection is receiving piperacillin-tazobactam, and cultures return a gram-negative bacillus. Which of the following organisms is expected to be covered by this agent?

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam covers Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, and Proteus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond its broad gram-positive coverage, piperacillin-tazobactam covers gram-negative organisms including Enterobacter species, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, and Proteus. Klebsiella pneumoniae therefore falls squarely within its spectrum. This is part of why it is a workhorse empiric agent for intra-abdominal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MRSA is the stated gram-positive exception to piperacillin-tazobactam coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycoplasma is an atypical pathogen treated with doxycycline, not with a β-lactam.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rickettsial organisms are treated first-line with doxycycline and are not covered by β-lactams.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus is not within its spectrum; tetracyclines are the class credited with VRE activity.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with a severe skin and soft tissue infection is receiving piperacillin-tazobactam but remains febrile. Blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following best explains the inadequate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Escherichia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Klebsiella species

choices.label: D
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Proteus species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam has broad gram-positive coverage except for MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam's gram-positive coverage is broad but explicitly excludes MRSA. When MRSA is isolated, an anti-MRSA agent must be used instead of relying on the β-lactam. Its gram-negative reach, by contrast, is one of the broadest available.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escherichia coli is covered by piperacillin-tazobactam.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Klebsiella is within its gram-negative spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus is among the gram-negative organisms it covers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin-tazobactam does cover Pseudomonas, which is one of its main advantages.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is hospitalized with bloody diarrhea and bacteremia, and blood cultures grow Campylobacter. Which of the following agents provides coverage of this organism in addition to broad gram-positive and gram-negative coverage?

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam's broad spectrum includes Pseudomonas and Campylobacter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam has broad gram-positive coverage (except MRSA) and very broad gram-negative coverage that includes Pseudomonas and Campylobacter. That breadth makes it suitable for initial empiric therapy in a septic patient before the organism is known. The other options are gram-positive agents or narrow penicillins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Linezolid is a gram-positive agent and would not treat a gram-negative enteric organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not effective against many gram-negative bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed, works only in the gut lumen, and has no gram-negative activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxacillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin aimed at gram-positive cocci, not enteric gram-negative rods.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: Blood cultures from a 66-year-old woman with pyelonephritis grow an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. Which of the following agents is the most reliable treatment?

explanation.summary: Carbapenems are the most reliable treatment for ESBL-producing bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbapenems are considered the most reliable treatment for infections caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing organisms. Their broad-spectrum activity and stability against β-lactamase enzymes is what preserves activity when other β-lactams are degraded. Meropenem is the only carbapenem among the options.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Linezolid covers gram-positive organisms and has no activity against a gram-negative bacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not effective against gram-negative bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin is readily degraded by β-lactamases and lacks the needed gram-negative spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin has no gram-negative coverage at all.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: An Escherichia coli isolate from a hospitalized patient is resistant to ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and several cephalosporins but remains susceptible to meropenem. Which of the following best explains this resistance pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism grows only under anaerobic conditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism has acquired a thick polysaccharide capsule

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism has lost its peptidoglycan cell wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism has mutated its 30S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism produces extended-spectrum β-lactamase enzymes

explanation.summary: ESBL producers make enzymes that degrade β-lactam antibiotics, leaving carbapenems as the reliable option.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing bacteria secrete β-lactamase enzymes that degrade other β-lactam antibiotics, which explains resistance across penicillins and cephalosporins. Carbapenems combine broad-spectrum activity with resistance to these enzymes, so they remain active. That is why carbapenems are the most reliable therapy for ESBL infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli is a facultative organism, and anaerobic growth does not explain β-lactam degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A capsule impairs phagocytosis but does not selectively inactivate β-lactam antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of the cell wall is not a feature of E. coli and would not spare carbapenem activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 30S mutation would affect aminoglycosides and tetracyclines, not β-lactams.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: Carbapenems are often summarized as covering essentially all gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Which of the following organisms is the important gram-positive exception to that rule?

explanation.summary: Carbapenems cover a wide range of gram-positive and gram-negative organisms except MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The shorthand for carbapenems is that they cover all gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, but MRSA is the explicit gram-positive exclusion. Anti-MRSA therapy must be added when that organism is suspected or isolated. The rest of the gram-positive and gram-negative spectrum is broad.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Haemophilus influenzae is a gram-negative organism covered by carbapenems, not the exception.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ESBL-producing Klebsiella is precisely the organism carbapenems treat most reliably.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methicillin-susceptible S. aureus is a gram-positive organism well within the carbapenem spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pneumoniae is covered by the broad gram-positive activity of carbapenems.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted with a pyogenic infection. The team selects a protein synthesis inhibitor. Under which condition are protein synthesis inhibitors most effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When host phagocytes have already engulfed most of the organisms

choices.label: B
choices.text: When the bacteria are actively dividing during acute infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: When the infection has become chronic and walled off by fibrosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: When the organism has formed a mature biofilm on a foreign body

choices.label: E
choices.text: When the organisms have entered a dormant, non-replicating state

explanation.summary: Protein synthesis inhibitors work best during the acute stage of infection, when bacteria are actively dividing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protein synthesis inhibitors act on the bacterial ribosome, so their effect depends on ongoing translation. Actively dividing organisms are synthesizing protein at a high rate and are therefore maximally susceptible. This is why these drugs are most effective during the acute stage of an infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phagocytosis is a host clearance mechanism and is not the condition that determines protein synthesis inhibitor efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A chronic, walled-off focus contains slowly metabolizing organisms and is the opposite of the acute stage favored here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Biofilm organisms are metabolically slowed and shielded, which reduces rather than enhances the effect of these agents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dormant, non-replicating organisms are translating minimally, so ribosome-directed drugs have little to act on.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A student is learning bacterial translation and notes that the ribosome contains three defined positions where individual amino acids are loaded and bonded, designated A, P, and E. Which set of names corresponds to these three letters?

explanation.summary: The three ribosomal sites are A (acceptor), P (peptidyl), and E (elongation).
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacterial ribosomes contain three sites important for peptide synthesis: A = acceptor, P = peptidyl, and E = elongation. Individual amino acids are loaded and bonded at these positions. Protein synthesis inhibitors act by interacting with these sites or with other parts of the ribosomal subunits.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Activation, polymerase, and extension describe other biochemical concepts, not the A, P, and E positions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anchor, priming, and exchange do not correspond to any of the three defined ribosomal sites.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticodon, primer, and editing are not the names given to the three ribosomal sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Attachment, processing, and excision are unrelated to the acceptor, peptidyl, and elongation sites.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: An investigator studies an antibiotic whose target lies within the small subunit of the bacterial ribosome. That subunit is built from a single ribosomal RNA molecule together with 21 associated proteins. Which ribosomal RNA is present in this subunit?

explanation.summary: The prokaryotic 30S subunit is composed of 16S rRNA plus 21 other proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The small ribosomal subunit in bacteria is the 30S subunit, and it is made up of 16S rRNA and 21 additional proteins. Aminoglycosides act at the 30S subunit and specifically target this 16S rRNA. Enzymatic modification of aminoglycosides prevents their interaction with the 16S rRNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5S rRNA is a component of the large 50S subunit, not the small subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 18S rRNA is a eukaryotic ribosomal RNA and is not part of the bacterial small subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 23S rRNA belongs to the 50S subunit and carries peptidyl transferase activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 28S rRNA is a eukaryotic ribosomal RNA and is not found in bacterial ribosomes.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: The large subunit of the 70S bacterial ribosome is responsible for forming the peptide bond between successive amino acids during protein synthesis. Which ribosomal RNA molecules compose this subunit?

explanation.summary: The 50S subunit is composed of 23S rRNA and 5S rRNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: In prokaryotes the large subunit is the 50S subunit, composed of 23S rRNA and 5S rRNA. It is the subunit important for forming the peptide bond between amino acids in protein synthesis. The 23S rRNA within it contains peptidyl transferase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 16S rRNA belongs to the small subunit, so this pairing spans two different subunits.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 16S rRNA is a component of the 30S small subunit, not of the large subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 18S and 28S rRNA are eukaryotic ribosomal RNAs and are absent from bacterial ribosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 28S rRNA is eukaryotic, so it cannot be part of the bacterial 50S subunit.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A bacterial mutant binds incoming charged tRNAs normally but cannot join successive amino acids into a growing polypeptide chain. The defect maps to the ribosomal RNA that carries peptidyl transferase activity. Which molecule is defective?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The initiator tRNA of the initiation complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: The messenger RNA at the acceptor site

explanation.summary: Peptidyl transferase, the enzyme that forms peptide bonds, resides in the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 23S rRNA contains peptidyl transferase, the enzyme that forms the peptide bonds between amino acids. A defect there permits tRNA binding but prevents bond formation. Chloramphenicol produces the same functional block by preventing transpeptidation at the 50S subunit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 16S rRNA is in the small subunit and is involved in decoding, not in peptide bond formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 5S rRNA is part of the 50S subunit but is not the molecule that carries peptidyl transferase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The initiator tRNA participates in initiation complex formation rather than in transpeptidation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Messenger RNA carries the coding sequence and has no catalytic role in peptide bond formation.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A medicinal chemist describes a class of antibacterial agents constructed from two or more amino sugars linked to a central aminocyclitol nucleus, with individual members differing in the amino sugars they carry. Which antibiotic class is described?

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides are composed of two or more amino sugars bonded to an aminocyclitol nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Structurally, aminoglycosides consist of two or more amino sugars bonded to an aminocyclitol nucleus, and the various aminoglycosides differ in which amino sugars they carry. These sugar moieties make the agents very hydrophilic, which is why they must be given intravenously.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrolides carry the suffix '-mycin' and include azithromycin, clarithromycin, and erythromycin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxazolidinones are represented by linezolid and are structurally unrelated to amino sugars.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Streptogramins comprise dalfopristin and quinupristin and do not share this aminocyclitol structure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tetracyclines are named for their four-ring structure and end in the suffix '-cycline', not for amino sugars.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a health care-associated gram-negative infection is to be started on an aminoglycoside. Which of the following drugs belongs to that class?

explanation.summary: Tobramycin is an aminoglycoside, alongside streptomycin, neomycin, gentamicin, and amikacin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Common examples of aminoglycosides include streptomycin, neomycin, gentamicin, tobramycin, and amikacin. All are 30S protein synthesis inhibitors. Because their structure contains sugar moieties they are very hydrophilic and are administered intravenously.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clindamycin is a lincosamide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxycycline is a second-generation tetracycline, a different 30S protein synthesis inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythromycin is a macrolide, identified by the '-mycin' suffix, acting at the 50S subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Linezolid is an oxazolidinone that binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: An intern asks why gentamicin cannot simply be prescribed as a tablet for an outpatient. Which property of aminoglycosides best explains the need for parenteral administration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dietary calcium chelates them within the gastric lumen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism removes them rapidly

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gastric acid degrades them into inactive ring fragments

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gut peptidases destroy them before absorption occurs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their sugar moieties make them hydrophilic and poorly absorbed

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides are highly hydrophilic because of their sugar moieties, so they are absorbed poorly and given IV or IM.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because their structure contains sugar moieties, aminoglycosides are very hydrophilic. Poor oral absorption follows, so these agents are administered intravenously or intramuscularly. They are then eliminated unchanged by the kidneys.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chelation by dietary cations is not the mechanism given for the parenteral route of aminoglycosides.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 30S ribosomal inhibitors are not substantially metabolized, so first-pass metabolism does not explain this.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acid degradation is not the stated limitation; poor absorption of a hydrophilic molecule is.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aminoglycosides are not peptides, and proteolysis in the gut is not the reason they are given parenterally.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action
